lessons.title: Causes and outline of the Second World War

lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain the long-term and immediate causes of the Second World War
Outline the main stages of the war
Describe Africa’s part in the war
reviewNotes: Verify: Versailles 1919; Wall Street Crash/Depression 1929; Hitler Chancellor January 1933; Munich 1938; invasion of Poland 1 Sept 1939; Pearl Harbor 7 Dec 1941; German surrender May 1945; Japan August–September 1945; Free France and Cameroon August 1940.
Teach Africa’s role according to the syllabus.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Causes
blocks.md: **Treaty of Versailles (1919):** many Germans felt it was harsh. **Great Depression** (from 1929): unemployment helped extreme parties. **Dictators:** Mussolini in Italy, **Hitler** (Chancellor from 1933) and aggressive expansion by Japan. **Weakness of the League of Nations:** failures over Manchuria (1931) and Abyssinia (1935). **Appeasement:** Britain and France made concessions, such as at Munich in 1938.

blocks.title: Outbreak and course
blocks.md: Germany invaded Poland on **1 September 1939**; Britain and France declared war two days later. Germany conquered much of Europe in 1939–41. In 1941 Germany invaded the Soviet Union, and Japan attacked Pearl Harbor (7 December), bringing in the USA. Germany surrendered in **May 1945**. Japan surrendered in **August–September 1945**, after atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

blocks.caption: From Versailles to the end of the Second World War.
blocks.alt: Timeline from 1919 to 1946 with 1919 Versailles, 1929 Depression, 1933 Hitler chancellor, 1939 war begins and 1945 war ends.

blocks.title: Africa
blocks.md: North Africa and the Horn were battlefields. Africans served as soldiers and labourers in Allied armies and supplied raw materials. In August 1940 French Cameroun and other parts of French Equatorial Africa declared for Free France under General de Gaulle. The war strengthened demands for change and weakened European powers, helping decolonisation.

blocks.title: Avoid errors
blocks.md:
- The Treaty of Versailles was one cause among several: do not blame it alone.
- Appeasement was not simple cowardice; it had domestic and strategic reasons.
- The war began in 1939 in Europe; for China and Japan, it began earlier.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Long-term versus short-term
blocks.statement: Classify as long-term cause or immediate trigger: (a) Treaty of Versailles, (b) invasion of Poland.
steps: (a) Signed in 1919, twenty years before: long-term.
(b) The event of 1 September 1939 led directly to Britain and France declaring war: immediate trigger.

blocks.title: Example 2 — League failure
blocks.statement: Explain how the League’s failure over Abyssinia encouraged aggression.
steps: The League’s sanctions were limited and did not stop Italy.
Dictators concluded that the League would not act firmly.

objectives: Define the Cold War and its origins
Describe key crises and the arms race
Explain the impact on Africa and the end of the Cold War
reviewNotes: Verify: Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan 1947; Berlin blockade 1948–49; NATO 1949; Warsaw Pact 1955; Berlin Wall 1961; Cuban Missile Crisis Oct 1962; Bandung 1955; Belgrade 1961; USSR dissolved December 1991.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: What was the Cold War?
blocks.md: The **Cold War** (about 1945–1991) was a rivalry between the **USA and its allies** (capitalism and liberal democracy) and the **USSR and its allies** (communism), fought without direct war between the two superpowers. It was waged by an **arms race**, alliances, propaganda, economic aid and **proxy wars** in other countries.

blocks.title: Main events
blocks.md: Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan (1947), Berlin blockade (1948–49), **NATO** (1949), Korean War (1950–53), **Warsaw Pact** (1955), the building of the Berlin Wall (1961), the **Cuban Missile Crisis** (1962), the Vietnam War, détente in the 1970s, the fall of the Berlin Wall (1989) and the dissolution of the USSR (December 1991).

blocks.caption: The two blocs in the Cold War.
blocks.alt: A table with the West led by the USA with NATO 1949 and the East led by the USSR with the Warsaw Pact 1955.

blocks.title: Africa and the Cold War
blocks.md: Both superpowers competed for influence in Africa, giving aid and arms and backing different sides in conflicts such as in Angola after 1975. Many new states joined the **Non-Aligned Movement** (the Bandung conference of 1955 for Asia and Africa; Belgrade in 1961). The end of the Cold War ended some superpower support and contributed to political change in the 1990s.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The two superpowers did not fight each other directly; the wars were proxy conflicts.
- NATO (1949) and the Warsaw Pact (1955) are different alliances.
- Non-alignment means not joining either bloc; it does not mean isolation.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Explain a proxy war
blocks.statement: Explain what a proxy war is, with an example from Africa.
steps: Two powers support opposing sides in another country’s conflict instead of fighting each other.
Example: Angola after 1975, where outside powers backed different groups.
This prolonged conflict and brought arms into the region.
blocks.answer: A conflict where superpowers back local sides.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Why non-alignment?
blocks.statement: Why did many new African and Asian states choose non-alignment?
steps: They wanted to avoid dependence on one superpower.
They hoped to receive aid from both sides.
blocks.answer: To keep independence of action and gain aid.
